query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, a thin FeNiCrCoCu coating doped with a minor fraction of aluminum forms and stabilizes a protective oxide tribo-layer, thereby reducing wear rates and friction compared to the undoped coating.
generation.material_initial_state: A micrometer-scale FeNiCrCoCu coating deposited on a steel substrate without aluminum addition.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a small Al fraction (e.g., 2–4 at.%) into the baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating to enhance oxide formation.
generation.conditions: Subject coated samples to pin-on-disk or similar tribological tests in air at temperatures ranging from room temperature up to ~800 °C, under normal loads up to ~20 N.
generation.structural_mediator: Al-stabilized surface oxide layer that forms during high-temperature sliding contact.
generation.mechanism: The doped coating preferentially forms a stable oxide scale at contact interfaces that protects against metal-to-metal contact and decreases wear and friction.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under temperatures above ~500 °C, the Al-doped coating will show measurably lower wear rates (e.g., a noticeable reduction relative to the undoped baseline) and decreased friction coefficients, corresponding to the development of a continuous protective oxide film.
generation.baseline: An undoped thin FeNiCrCoCu coating of similar thickness and grain size deposited on the same substrate and tested under the same loads and temperatures.
generation.boundary: Applies for high-temperature applications (up to ~800 °C) with moderate contact loads (≤20 N) in oxidizing atmospheres. Effects at lower temperatures or in inert atmospheres are not fully characterized here.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative improvement in wear resistance depends on the specific Al concentration, testing atmosphere, and coating microstructure; exact magnitude of effect remains to be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on the same substrate: one with ~3 at.% Al and a control without Al. Perform identical high-temperature wear tests (e.g., using pin-on-disk) at multiple temperatures up to ~800 °C. Characterize oxide thickness and composition via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of the worn surfaces.
measurements: Wear rates (e.g., volume loss) and friction coefficients at different temperatures for doped vs. undoped coatings
Thickness and continuity of oxide layers via cross-sectional SEM/EDS
Comparative surface topography changes with 3D profilometry
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped coating does not form a more protective oxide layer or shows no measurable improvement in wear resistance relative to the baseline coating at elevated temperatures, the hypothesis is falsified.

Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

Development of materials suitable for molten fluoride salt environments started in the 1950s with the Aircraft Reactor Experiment (ARE) [4] . This experiment used Inconel 6

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. chosen.lever: Incremental temperature range (e.g., 25–800 °C) at prescribed normal loads
chosen.technique: Systematic high-temperature pin-on-disk wear tests and microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM, EDS)
chosen.conditions: FeNiCrCoCu coatings (a few micrometers thick) applied to steel substrates tested under loads up to 20 N in air or controlled atmosphere
chosen.why: We hypothesize that the dominant factor governing the overall wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin coatings under high-temperature conditions is the formation and stability of a protective oxide tribo-layer. Intervention: incorporate controlled doping of a minor alloying element (e.g., Al) into a baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating to promote more robust oxide formation. Predicted observations: under temperatures above 500 °C and loads up to 20 N, doped coatings will exhibit lower wear rates and reduced friction coefficients, consistent with enhanced oxide scale formation and protective coverage. Prior studies at room temperature show that oxidation can improve tribological behavior, but a comprehensive multi-temperature regime has yet to be tested. This study addresses that gap by directly linking oxide film stability to wear resistance at elevated temperatures. The hypothesis would be falsified if no stable oxide film develops or if wear resistance does not improve despite doping and elevated temperatures, indicating that oxide effects are not the primary controlling mechanism for wear resistance.
